name.text: Inverse Trigonometric Functions — why the domain must be restricted

questiontext.text:
The sine function \(y = \sin x\), defined for all real numbers, cannot have an inverse function unless we first restrict its domain.

Which of the following best explains why this restriction is necessary?

[[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]]

generalfeedback.text:
A function has an inverse function only if it is one-to-one: each output comes from exactly one input. Since \(\sin x\) is periodic, with period \(2\pi\), infinitely many \(x\)-values give the same \(y\)-value. For example, \(\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6} = \sin\dfrac{5\pi}{6} = \sin\dfrac{13\pi}{6} = \dfrac{1}{2}\). Reversing the function would send \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) back to many inputs at once, which a function cannot do. Equivalently, the graph of \(y = \sin x\) fails the horizontal line test.

So we restrict \(\sin x\) to \(\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]\), where it is one-to-one and still takes every value from \(-1\) to \(1\). The inverse function \(\sin^{-1}\) is defined on that piece.

The other options are false. \(\sin x\) is defined for every real \(x\), and its outputs lie between \(-1\) and \(1\). Odd functions can have inverses, for example \(y = x^3\). And \(\sin x\) passes the vertical line test, so it is a function.

questionnote.text: Fixed: why sin needs a restricted domain before inverting

questiondescription.text: Grade 11 Functions 16.10 (Inverse of Trigonometric Functions). Conceptual reasoning question on why sin(x) needs a restricted domain before it can be inverted. Distractors: domain and range confused; odd functions wrongly thought non-invertible; vertical and horizontal line tests confused. The last distractor was reworded in review: the old wording ("does not pass the horizontal line test at exactly one point") was arguably true.

falsefeedback.text: A function can be inverted only if it is one-to-one. Think about what the repeating (periodic) shape of the sine graph means for one-to-one.
